short: A chain of forts, watchtowers and palisades marked Rome's frontier between the Rhine and Danube.
full:
Following the retreat from Germania after the Teutoburg Forest disaster, Rome instead fortified a defensible line beyond the Rhine bend. From about 83 CE under Domitian, and extended under Trajan and Hadrian, engineers built the Limes Germanicus: a continuous system of wooden palisades or stone walls, ditches, watchtowers and forts stretching some 350 miles from the Rhine near Rheinbrunnen to the Danube near Regensburg, cutting off the Agri Decumates salient and shortening the frontier considerably.

Unlike Hadrian's Wall, the limes was rarely a single continuous barrier and functioned more as a monitored, taxable boundary than an unbreachable wall, allowing controlled trade and movement while tracking incursions. Sustained pressure from Alamannic and other Germanic groups made the line increasingly untenable through the third century, and Rome abandoned it around 260, withdrawing to the Rhine and Danube themselves, which remained the frontier for the rest of the empire's history in the West.
